title: Sharing behavior
summary: Traits declare what a type can do, so one function can do it for many types.

blocks.html: A circle and a rectangle have nothing in common except the thing we care about: both have an area. A trait is the name we give that shared behavior. It declares method signatures and nothing else; each type then says how those methods work for it.

blocks.title: a Shape trait

blocks.html:
trait Shape is a contract: any type that claims to be a Shape can answer area(). The claim is written impl Shape for Circle, and the compiler holds you to it — forget the method and it stops you before the program runs: error[E0046]: not all trait items implemented, missing: `area`.

Some methods have an obvious default body. Declare it in the trait and implementors get it for free, unless they override it. Inside a default method self is the concrete value, so it can call the methods the type does implement.

blocks.title: a default method
blocks.output:
a shape with area 12.57
a shape with area 2.00

blocks.html: Now the payoff. A generic function says "I take any T" and a bound says what that T must be able to do: T: Shape. One function, written once, works for every shape that exists or ever will. Two abilities are joined with +, or listed in a where clause when the signature gets crowded. std::fmt::Debug is the trait behind {:?}, and #[derive(Debug)] has the compiler write it for us.

blocks.title: one bound and two bounds
blocks.output:
total 15.71
Rect { width: 2.0, height: 3.0 } has area 6.00

blocks.html: #[derive(Debug)] is not magic, it is a shortcut. Debug, Clone, and PartialEq are ordinary traits, and deriving one tells the compiler to write the boring impl — print the fields, copy the fields, compare the fields. Deriving PartialEq is what makes == work on your struct. One catch: every field must already implement the trait you asked to derive, or the compiler refuses.

blocks.title: derive writes the impls

blocks.html: Writing <T: Shape> on every function is noise when the bound is obvious. impl Trait in argument position means the same thing: fn show(shape: impl Shape). In return position it means "some concrete type that implements Shape, and I am not telling you which" — one type per function, chosen by the body.

blocks.title: impl Trait, both positions

blocks.html: A vector holding circles and rectangles cannot be Vec<T>, because a vector holds one type. Box<dyn Shape> solves it: a box owns a value on the heap, and dyn Shape says "whatever is in here implements Shape". The compiler stops tracking the concrete type, and the method is looked up when the program runs. That is dynamic dispatch. The generic version above is the opposite: the compiler stamps out a separate copy of the function for each type, so each call is a direct one. That is called monomorphization.

blocks.title: a vector of shapes

quiz.q: What does a trait declaration contain?
options: Method signatures, and optionally default bodies
The fields every implementor must have
The values of the constants used by the type
quiz.why: A trait describes behavior: which methods exist and what they take and return. Fields belong to structs, and each implementor keeps its own.

quiz.q: A generic function bounded by T: Shape is called with a slice of circles. When is the code that runs Shape::area chosen for that call?
options: At compile time, because T is a known concrete type
At run time, by looking up the method on the value
Never: the bound only documents intent
quiz.why: A generic function is monomorphized: the compiler produces a version specialized for Circle, so the call is direct. A trait object instead looks the method up at run time.

quiz.q: You want == to work on your struct. Which line gives you that?
quiz.why: PartialEq is the trait behind ==, and deriving it has the compiler write a field-by-field comparison. Clone only adds the .clone() method.

exercise.brief: Triangle already implements Area, but with the wrong formula: it adds the sides instead of using half of base times height. Fix the body so the program prints the real area.
exercise.hint: Inside the impl, self is the triangle, so self.base and self.height are the fields. The area of a triangle is base * height / 2.0, not the sum of the two sides.
